explanations.E0140:
# E0140: instantiations that never end

A generic function, class or enum cannot use itself with a type argument that grows, directly or through other declarations: `f([x])` inside `fn f<T>(x: T)` calls `f` with `[T]` for `T`, and a field of type `Nest<[T]>` inside `Nest<T>` does the same for a type.

## Why

Each set of type arguments a program uses gets its own compiled copy of the declaration. A copy for `i64` that uses one for `[i64]`, which uses one for `[[i64]]`, would need copies without end, so the compiler reports the cycle instead. A use with the same arguments, such as `f(x)` inside `f`, needs no new copy, and a growing use that never comes back to its declaration, such as `g([x])` in `f` for a `g` that does not use `f`, needs one.

A call through a bound can close a cycle too. A call `t.wrap(x)` on a type parameter calls the method of each type that `wrap` can reach, so the argument of the call counts as an argument of each of those methods. When one of them calls the function again with a longer argument, as `go(self, [x])` does, the instantiations never end.

A conformance can close a cycle too. A call `x.run()` on a type parameter can reach the method of every type that conforms to the interface, so the compiler counts a call through `Run` as a call of each of them. A conformance for a type like `Box<T>` takes one level off the type, as the receiver of the call is a `Box<T>` and the method knows `T`. When a method of `Box<T>` calls a function that calls `run` again with a `Box<Box<T>>`, the type grows by two levels and shrinks by one, and the instantiations never end. The error names the method that the cycle runs, and says that the call counts as reaching every conformance. The rule is cautious: it cannot see which conformance a call reaches, so it can report a cycle that would stop.

An operator can close a cycle too. `==` on a class or an enum with a written `eq` calls that `eq`, and `==` on an array, an optional or an enum calls the `eq` of each type inside it. In a generic body, the compiler counts `==`, `<` and `contains` on a type that names a type parameter as a call through `Eq` or `Ord`, which reaches every conformance. When the `eq` of `W<T>` compares two values of type `W<[T]>`, the type grows, and the instantiations never end. An array or an optional of `T` has its levels taken off first, as the compiler writes its `eq` and adds no growth by itself.

The error names what the program writes at the place: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` or `contains`. The help says that the operator is a call through `Eq` or `Ord`, and that a call through it counts as reaching every conformance. An enum with no written `eq` has a generated one. When the cycle runs through it, the label says "the `==` of `E` compares `W<T>`", and underlines the payload type.

`print` can close a cycle in the same way. `print` of a class or an enum with a written `to_string` calls that `to_string`, and `print` of an array, an optional or an enum calls the `to_string` of each type inside it. In a generic body, the compiler counts `print` of a type that names a type parameter as a call through `Display`. When the `to_string` of `W<T>` prints a value of type `W<[T]>`, the type grows, and the instantiations never end.

The error names `print`, `eprint` or the interpolation, and underlines the part of the string that the interpolation shows. For the generated `to_string` of an enum, the label says "the `to_string` of `E` shows `W<T>`".

An associated type can close a cycle. A value of type `S.Item` is the type that the conformance of `S` chose for `Item`, and a choice such as `Chain<Chain<Chain<T>>>` is a type that has more levels than its target `Chain<T>`. A function that passes an `S.Item` on, or calls a method of one, instantiates itself with a longer type, and the instantiations never end. A choice that names no type parameter, as `type Child = Dir`, does not grow, so a call with an `S.Child` is fine. The growth of a choice that names another associated type is counted with the growth of that type.

A field that holds an associated type can close a cycle too. A field of type `T.Item` holds the type that the conformance of `T` chose for `Item`. When that choice names the class or enum again with a longer type argument, as `type Item = E<W<W<T>>>` does for the enum `E<T: I>` that holds `T.Item`, the type grows with each use, and the instantiations never end. The error names the class or enum that holds the field, shows the choice, and a note shows the field. A choice that names the type with the same or a shorter argument, or that names no type parameter, does not grow.

Three rules apply to this form.

- A choice is for one list of interface arguments. A conformance to `S<bool>` is not one to `S<i64>`, so a choice that grows for `S<bool>` gives no error to a field of type `T.Item` with `T: S<i64>`.
- A link of a chain such as `T.Next.Item` can grow without end for the arguments of the use. The compiler then reads the base `T` without that link, so the other links still count.
- A link before the associated type narrows the choices. In `T.Other.Item`, the compiler reads the choices of `Item` only in the classes and enums that a choice of `Other` names. When no choice of `Other` names the class of a growing choice, the field gives no error. The compiler does not follow the class from one turn of the cycle to the next, so it can report a cycle that would stop.
  In two cases the compiler cannot find the classes that the link names, and the use counts as every choice of `Item`. First, a choice of `Other` is not a class or an enum. It can be a type parameter, an associated type, an array, an optional, or no type at all. Second, the compiler must read more than 64 classes, enums and choices to find the choices that the use can mean. It counts each class or enum that a choice of `Other` names as one. It counts each choice of `Item` that such a class makes as one.

The error says that the check is cautious. A use such as `T.Other.Item` counts as each choice that a conformance makes. The only exception is a choice that the check can show to be impossible.

A query that asks whether a type conforms to an interface can run too deep. Each class or enum type that the query checks stays open until the types inside it are checked. When more than 262144 of them are open, one inside the other, the compiler stops the query. It reports the stop once for each class or enum, at its name. The message names the interface and the type that the query began with: "the check of `Eq` for `E0<i64>` stopped after 262144 nested types". A declaration that instantiates itself without end, through a path that the other rules do not see, makes a query like this. A valid program can reach the limit only when its types nest more than 262144 levels, and no program written by hand does.

## Broken

```sisu
fn nest<T>(x: T, n: i64) {
    if n > 0 {
        nest([x], n - 1)
    }
}

fn main() {
    nest(1, 3)
}
```

## Fixed

```sisu
fn nest<T>(x: T, n: i64) {
    if n > 0 {
        nest(x, n - 1)
    }
}

fn main() {
    nest(1, 3)
}
```
